Freak Out
FREEK OWT
verb / noun (Boomer slang)
From freak (Old English frician, to dance, is doubtful; more likely a dialect word for a sudden whim or caprice, 1560s) + out. Freak out appears in mid-1960s drug culture for a panicked or wildly excited reaction, and was put on the map by Frank Zappa and the Mothers of Invention’s debut album Freak Out! (1966). By the 1970s it meant simply to panic, to lose one’s cool, or to become extremely upset — the sense every grandchild knows. Chic’s disco hit "Le Freak" ("Freak out!", 1978) made it a dance-floor shout.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To freak out is to lose control — to panic, to fly into a rage, or to come unglued with fear or excitement. In 1966 it described a reaction to drugs; by 1978 it was a disco chant; today it is how every teenager describes his parents’ reaction to a dented fender. The Christian observation: the word names a real and common experience, and Scripture addresses it with tenderness and with command. The disciples freaked out in the boat on the Sea of Galilee while the Lord slept; He rose, said to the sea, "Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm" (Mar 4:39), and then turned to them: "Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith?" (Mar 4:40). The antidote to freaking out is not a technique but a trust: "What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee" (Psa 56:3). "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus" (Php 4:6–7). The promise is not that storms will never come but that a mind "stayed on thee" will be kept "in perfect peace" (Isa 26:3). A father who does not freak out when his son confesses a failure has preached that sermon without words.

Webster 1828 Definition

Boomer slang (mid-1960s; Zappa’s Freak Out!, 1966) for losing control in panic, anger, or excitement — answered by the Lord who stilled the storm and asked, "Why are ye so fearful?" (Mar 4:40).

expand to see more

FREAK OUT, v.i. and v.t. (Boomer slang, mid-1960s–present) 1. To react with sudden panic, anger, or wild excitement; to lose emotional control. 2. To cause someone to do so. "Don’t freak out." "The noise freaked me out." n. freak-out, an episode of losing control; originally a drug-induced one.

Webster (1828) — FREAK, noun 1. Literally, a sudden starting or change of place. Hence, 2. A sudden causeless change or turn of the mind; a whim or fancy; a capricious prank. She is restless and peevish, and sometimes in a freak will instantly change her habitation.

Decode for families: one of the most durable Boomer words — your children use it daily.

Key Scripture

Mar 4:39 — "And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm."

Mar 4:40 — "And he said unto them, Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith?"

Psa 56:3 — "What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee."

Php 4:6 — "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God."

Isa 26:3 — "Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee."

Modern Corruption

The word normalizes the loss of self-control as an ordinary reaction; Scripture treats fear and rage as storms the Lord commands to be still, and the mind stayed on Him as kept in perfect peace.

expand to see more

In the 1960s the freak-out was half a goal. A good concert, a good dose, a good happening was supposed to make you lose control. The ecstatic loss of self was prized. By the time the word reached the suburbs it had lost the glamour and kept the license: freaking out became a normal, even expected, way to respond to bad news. Scripture does not share that expectation. "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city" (Pro 16:32). Self-control is a fruit of the Spirit, not a symptom of repression.

But Scripture is gentle with the frightened. The Lord did not leave the disciples in the boat; He got up. Paul does not merely say "Be careful for nothing"; he says what to do instead — pray with thanksgiving — and promises a peace that guards the heart (Php 4:6–7). The grandparent who teaches a grandchild Psalm 56:3 has given him something better than "calm down."

Greek & Hebrew Roots

16th-c. English freak (a sudden whim, caprice) → 19th-c. freak (an oddity) → mid-1960s freak out (drug panic) → 1970s general "lose control."

expand to see more

1560s English freak — a sudden turn of mind, a caprice (perhaps from Old English frician, to dance)

19th c.: freak — a malformed creature; freak of nature; the circus freak show

Mid-1960s: freak out — a panicked or ecstatic reaction, especially on drugs

1966: Frank Zappa and the Mothers of Invention, Freak Out!

1978: Chic, "Le Freak" — "Freak out!" as a disco shout

Usage

""Don’t freak out, Mom, it’s just a scratch.""

"Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith? (Mar 4:40)."

"What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee (Psa 56:3)."
